entities.summary:
Uruguay, officially the Oriental Republic of Uruguay, is the smallest country in South America by area, located on the Atlantic coast between Brazil and Argentina. With 3.5 million people in 176,215 km², Uruguay has consistently ranked as Latin America's most stable democracy, most equal society, and most secular state — a combination that has made it exceptional in the Latin American context.

The territory was inhabited by the Charrúa and Guaraní peoples before Spanish colonization. It served as a contested buffer zone between Spanish (Buenos Aires) and Portuguese (Brazil) colonial empires. José Artigas led the Artiguista revolution (1810s) seeking independence and agrarian reform; after a period of Brazilian annexation (1821–1825), Uruguay declared independence in 1828 with British diplomatic support as a buffer state between Argentina and Brazil.

Uruguay's 20th century was shaped by the reformist governments of José Batlle y Ordóñez (1903–1915) who established universal suffrage, workers' rights, public education, and state enterprise — making Uruguay Latin America's first welfare state. The Tupamaros guerrilla movement (1960s–70s) and the military dictatorship (1973–1985) interrupted democratic rule. Since democratization, Uruguay has undertaken a series of progressive social reforms: legalizing abortion (2012), same-sex marriage (2013), and marijuana (2013) — making it the world's first country to fully legalize cannabis under state control. President José Mujica (2010–2015), a former Tupamaro guerrilla who donated 90% of his salary to charity, became a global symbol of political authenticity.
